```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r setup}
library(mysteryroster)
td_backend <- attribute_truth_backends()
td_available <- isTRUE(td_backend$available[td_backend$backend == "truthdiscovery"])
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = td_available)
```

`vignette("truth-fusion")` covers `method = "majority"` (R-native);
`vignette("truth-fusion-crowdkit")` covers `method = "dawid_skene"`/
`"one_coin_dawid_skene"` (optional, via `crowd-kit`). This vignette covers
the third and, for now, last backend: `method = "sums"`, `"average_log"`,
`"investment"`, `"pooled_investment"`, and `"truthfinder"`, via the
`joesingo/truthdiscovery` Python package.

```{r availability-note, eval = TRUE}
td_backend[td_backend$backend == "truthdiscovery", ]
```

## A licensing note before anything else

`crowd-kit` is Apache-2.0; `truthdiscovery` is **GPL-3.0**. mysteryroster
itself is MIT licensed and does not vendor or incorporate any
`truthdiscovery` source -- `.mysteryroster_truthdiscovery_fit()` only calls
the package a user has installed, at arm's length, through `reticulate`,
exactly as it would call any other optional runtime dependency. If you
redistribute a bundle that includes the actual `truthdiscovery` package
alongside mysteryroster, GPL-3.0's copyleft terms apply to *that bundle*;
they do not convert mysteryroster's own source. This is a factual
description of how the dependency is used, not legal advice -- get a real
legal review before any formal redistribution (a CRAN submission that
bundles Python dependencies, for instance).

A second, practical note: `truthdiscovery`'s last release predates
Python's removal of `distutils`, so `pip install truthdiscovery` fails at
build time on Python >= 3.12 (`ModuleNotFoundError: No module named
'distutils'`), even though the installed package runs fine once it is
actually installed into an older interpreter (this was verified directly,
against Python 3.11). If you want both this backend and `crowd_kit`
available at once, they currently need **separate** Python environments.

If `available` is `FALSE` above, `attribute_truth_fusion(method =
"truthfinder", ...)` errors with that exact reason -- never a silent
fall-back to `"majority"` -- and the code below is shown but not executed.

## The same simulated panel, three backends

Same 16 simulated NPIs as `vignette("truth-fusion-crowdkit")`: `source_1`
correct on 15 of 16, `source_2` always correct, `source_3` a pure
false-positive-biased source that always reports `"active"` regardless of
the true status.

```{r simulate}
entities <- 1:16
true_status <- ifelse(entities %% 2 == 1, "active", "inactive")
claims <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(entities), function(i) {
  e <- entities[i]
  t <- true_status[i]
  source_1 <- if (e == 6) "active" else t
  data.frame(
    entity_id = as.character(e), attribute = "status",
    source_id = c("source_1", "source_2", "source_3"),
    claimed_value = c(source_1, t, "active"), reference_year = 2024
  )
}))
```

```{r fit-sums}
sums_result <- attribute_truth_fusion(claims, method = "sums")
sums_result
unique(sums_result$source_diagnostics[c("source_id", "reliability_score")])
```

Like the Crowd-Kit backend, `"sums"` fits once, jointly, across all 16
entity-years, and correctly puts `source_3`'s trust score well below the
other two -- but `source_diagnostics$true_label`/`observed_label`/
`error_probability` are all `NA` here. `truthdiscovery`'s trust-propagation
algorithms estimate a single scalar trust per source, never a full
confusion matrix; only `crowd-kit`'s `"dawid_skene"` does that.

## Belief scores are explicitly uncalibrated -- not probabilities

```{r score-type}
sums_result$predictions$score_type[1]
```

`score_type = "uncalibrated_belief"`, never `"posterior_probability"`.
This is not a cautious label applied just in case -- it reflects a
directly verified property of these algorithms. `crowd-kit`'s `probas_`
sum to 1 across a task's candidate values, because it is modeling a
genuine categorical posterior; `truthdiscovery`'s belief update is not
normalized that way:

```{r uncalibrated-check}
tf_result <- attribute_truth_fusion(claims, method = "truthfinder")
entity_6 <- tf_result$candidate_scores[tf_result$candidate_scores$entity_id == "6", ]
entity_6[, c("candidate_value", "vote_share")]
sum(entity_6$vote_share)
```

`"active"` and `"inactive"` belief for entity 6 sum to well over 1 --
`TruthFinder`'s belief scores are a confidence measure the algorithm
itself defines, not a probability distribution. Treat `model_score` as a
within-algorithm ranking signal, never as a calibrated chance of being
correct.

## Convergence is not guaranteed at this package's default settings

```{r pooled-investment-default, warning = TRUE}
default_pi <- attribute_truth_fusion(claims, method = "pooled_investment")
default_pi$model_diagnostics[, c("converged", "n_iterations")]
all(default_pi$predictions$abstained)
```

This is a real, reproducible finding, not a contrived example:
`"pooled_investment"`, with this package's shared default
(`max_iterations = 100`), genuinely fails to converge on this fixture --
`truthdiscovery` raises rather than returning a partial result, so every
prediction abstains with `abstention_reason = "model_did_not_converge"`.
Raising `max_iterations` resolves it here:

```{r pooled-investment-raised}
raised_pi <- attribute_truth_fusion(claims, method = "pooled_investment", max_iterations = 500L)
raised_pi$model_diagnostics[, c("converged", "n_iterations")]
```

It converges at 109 iterations on this data -- comfortably under 500, but
over this package's default of 100. Always check
`model_diagnostics$converged` rather than assuming the default is enough;
this is exactly the kind of silent-looking failure (an all-abstained
result, not a crash) that is easy to miss if you don't check.

## Diagnostics shared with the Crowd-Kit backend

`n_disconnected_components > 1` carries the same meaning as it does for
`dawid_skene`/`one_coin_dawid_skene`: sources in different components
share no task in common, so their estimated trust is not jointly
identifiable from this call alone.

```{r disconnected, warning = TRUE}
disconnected_claims <- data.frame(
  entity_id = c("1", "1", "2", "2"), attribute = "state",
  source_id = c("a", "b", "c", "d"),
  claimed_value = c("CO", "CO", "NM", "NM"), reference_year = 2024
)
attribute_truth_fusion(disconnected_claims, method = "sums")$model_diagnostics[
  , "n_disconnected_components"
]
```

`on_source_conflict = "multi_value"` is rejected for every method in this
backend, for the same reason as the Crowd-Kit backend: these algorithms
assume exactly one claim per source-task.

```{r multi-value-error, error = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
attribute_truth_fusion(claims, method = "sums", on_source_conflict = "multi_value")
```

## `implication_function`: evaluated, disabled by default

TruthFinder's original design lets belief in one claim influence belief in
a related claim -- for example, two candidate addresses close enough to
plausibly be a rounding or transcription variant of the same real
location. `truthdiscovery` exposes this as `implication_function`, and
`attribute_truth_fusion()` passes an R function straight through to it:

```{r implication}
no_op_implication <- function(var, val1, val2) 0
with_implication <- attribute_truth_fusion(
  claims, method = "truthfinder", implication_function = no_op_implication
)
identical(with_implication$predictions, tf_result$predictions)
```

A no-op implication (always `0`, meaning "no influence between any two
claims") reproduces the plain result exactly, confirming the passthrough
itself does not silently change anything. This package deliberately
**does not** ship a geographic-distance implication function, and
`implication_function` defaults to `NULL` (disabled) -- per the project's
own phase plan, geographic similarity is evaluated as a mechanism here,
not yet built out as a feature, and ordinary TruthFinder should be
compared against majority voting and Dawid-Skene on its own merits before
any geographic extension is layered on top. Every call also crosses the
R/Python boundary for each pair of claims being compared, so a non-trivial
implication function will be slow on large datasets.

## What this does and doesn't establish

Exactly as with the Crowd-Kit backend: `"sums"`, `"average_log"`,
`"investment"`, `"pooled_investment"`, and `"truthfinder"` are a reliable,
optional backend -- not yet a validated source of truth, and not yet
compared against real held-out physician-location data. They can rank a
degenerate, always-wrong-on-negatives source correctly (the first example
above); they can also fail to converge at this package's own default
settings without any crash to announce it (the second example) --
inspect `model_diagnostics` rather than trusting a result just because it
returned. No accuracy claim is made here, or should be made from this
vignette alone, about whether any of these methods out-performs
`"majority"` at the actual task this package exists for -- that is
explicitly the next phase of work, once a held-out validation dataset
exists.
